title: The white hawk
hook: tradition remembers him with a white hawk and a blue horse

segments.voice: Yesterday, his letters: written orders carried to sangats far away. Your line was a guru's letters. Did your note find its way to someone? Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

Look at a Sikh painting of Guru Gobind Singh, on a calendar in a kitchen, on the wall of a gurdwara hall, in an old book. Often he is on horseback. The horse is shown blue-gray. And on his raised hand, wearing a glove, sits a white hawk. Sikh songs call him by those two things. In Punjabi he is the one with the white hawk, and the rider of the blue horse. A teacher remembered by a bird and a horse. Today, why.
screen: `A PAINTING ON A KITCHEN WALL.` → `A BLUE HORSE, A WHITE HAWK.` → `REMEMBERED BY A BIRD.`

segments.voice: Start with the plain meaning. In the world the Guru lived in, a trained hawk on the wrist belonged to rulers and nobles. Hunting with hawks was a royal pastime. So a Guru with a hawk is a Guru who carries himself like a sovereign. That fits what we've been reading in his own writings: a man who writes to an emperor as an equal, who calls his followers to stand up straight, unafraid. Some Sikhs read the hawk as saying, without a word, this community bows only to God. Now the color. A white hawk is striking, and the songs dwell on it. Some Sikhs hear white as a picture of purity: power held with a clean heart. The hawk is fierce, it hunts, but it comes back to the glove. Strength that answers to someone. Then the horse. Tradition gives him a blue horse, and the image runs straight into Sikh life. Blue is a color some Khalsa Sikhs wear in their turbans and robes, and the Nihang Sikhs, who keep the old martial ways, are known for it. Riders on horseback still lead some Sikh processions. Here's the honest line. These are memories carried in paintings, songs and stories, not details the Guru records about himself. Tradition holds them, and Sikhs treasure them. What they do is give a face to an idea. A teacher of the One, mounted and ready, with a wild bird that chooses to come back to his hand.
screen: `A HAWK ON THE WRIST: SOVEREIGNTY.` · `WHITE: POWER WITH A CLEAN HEART.` · `THE BLUE HORSE IN SIKH LIFE.` · `MEMORIES IN SONG, NOT HIS OWN RECORD.` · then, large: `THE HAWK AND THE HORSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a bird fly. If you can, go to a window or step outside and find one bird, any bird. Follow it with your eyes, as long as it lets you. Notice how it uses the air instead of fighting it. Notice where it lands. If there's no bird in sight, close your eyes and picture the white hawk leaving the glove, circling, and coming back. If you pray, you can let the name Waheguru ride along on each breath while you watch. The bell holds the time.
The white hawk. In paintings and songs, Guru Gobind Singh rides a blue horse with a white hawk on his hand: a sovereign bearing, held with a clean heart. Today's word.
Your line: the hawk and the horse. Today, when you feel strong about something, do what the hawk does: go out fully, and come back to the hand. Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

fork.setup: you're painting the Tenth Guru for a gurdwara wall. what does tradition put on his raised hand?
fork.reveal: a white hawk, sitting on a gloved hand: a sign of sovereignty, in a bird that comes back.

original.note: Punjabi: a hawk. Songs call the Guru the one with the white hawk.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pet bird in an old painting.
what it means: a hawk on the wrist was a ruler's sign. the Guru's bearing says this community bows only to God.
what a scholar hears: an image held by painting, song and story, not by the Guru's own writings; tradition treasures it all the same.
